aions_core/claude_aions_bridge.py: This file connects the AIONS knowledge retrieval system with Claude's language model to provide fast, accurate answers. It takes user questions and tries to find matching information from a vector database first (the CBMS system), and if that fails, falls back to the language model for help. The main job is measuring how well the hybrid approach works by tracking response time, what information chunks were used, and overall performance quality. It receives a query string as input and returns a response dictionary containing the answer text, the source that provided it, how long it took in milliseconds, how many reference pieces were used, and whether performance was excellent or good. The code imports and calls the smart_cbms_response function to do the actual retrieval work. Someone searching for how Claude integrates with the AIONS system, or looking for where hybrid retrieval responses come from, would find this file.
aions_core/server/refgraph.py: This file builds and maintains a flexible web of connections that tracks how different pieces of knowledge reference each other across the system. Instead of requiring exact matches for references (which breaks when files move or get renamed), it uses multiple fallback strategies that gradually lower their confidence levels: exact ID matches score highest at 1.0, manifest entries score 0.95, parked chunks score 0.80, normalized matches score 0.75, file path matches score 0.70, concept matches score 0.60, and token-based semantic overlap scores 0.30-0.55, with unresolved references kept as hints at 0.00. The system takes a directory path to chunks (individual knowledge units), an optional quarantine folder for archived pieces, a knowledge manifest file listing known IDs, and a project root directory for file indexing. It outputs statistics about how resolved the graph is, which chunks are at risk of depending on archived material, what other chunks reference a given ID, and more. It can be used from the command line with various flags like --stats, --who-refs, --resolve, --unresolved, or --build-index to generate detailed reports. The code has no external dependencies beyond Python's standard library and works with JSON files stored in folders. Someone wanting to verify that all their knowledge pieces are properly connected, find broken or weak links in the knowledge base, or check which documents depend on a specific piece of information would search for this file.
aions_core/tools/analyze_csv.py: This file reads a large comma-separated values file and categorizes what it contains, particularly looking for where data chunks are stored and tracking the locations of critical system files. It scans through a CSV file that lists file paths, groups them by parent directory when they have .json in the name and appear to be chunks, and maintains a separate list of critical file locations including crla_core.py, pocket_qc.py, plasters_loader.py, AIONS_ULTIMATE_UNIFIED.py, and knowledge_manifest.json. The tool takes the path to a CSV file as input and prints human-readable reports showing the top 20 chunk storage locations with their counts and where each critical file was found (up to 5 results per file shown, with counts indicating how many times each was found). It uses Python's built-in CSV reader and dictionary data structures to organize results. Someone investigating the layout of the knowledge system, trying to understand where all the data pieces are stored, tracking down copies of critical files, or auditing the structure of a full system scan would use this tool.
aions_core/unified_core.py: This file creates a unified interface that combines seven specialized systems (core knowledge engine, vector search enhancement, hybrid retrieval, Claude bridge, agent task execution, style profiles, and monitoring) into one cohesive system while maintaining backward compatibility with the previous version. It starts by attempting to load each component and reports which ones succeeded; components that fail to load are simply skipped rather than breaking the whole system. The main entry point is the AIONSv2 class, which can be initialized with flags to enable or disable specific features and whether to fall back to the older version if something goes wrong. When processing a query, the system first checks a safety guardrail against hallucination, then selects the best processing mode (hybrid retrieval, vector search, or core engine), optionally applies a style to the answer, and logs everything to the monitoring dashboard. Input is a user query string and various optional settings; output is a response dictionary containing the answer, metadata about which systems provided it, execution time, evidence used, and more. The file imports from multiple internal modules including the vector enhancement, hybrid retrieval, Claude bridge, agent layer, style parameters, monitoring, and generative AI components. Someone wanting to understand how all the AIONS systems work together, launch the complete system, run performance benchmarks, or get health status of all components would consult this file.
control_plane/agents/agent_runner.py: This file enables specialized worker roles to execute tasks safely by restricting them to only the actions their job description allows. When a goal comes in for a specific role (like a Linux administrator or a file manager), the runner creates a filtered view of available actions based on fnmatch patterns in the role's allowed_skills list, then either tries to use a small language model to plan the next steps or falls back to a simple lexical search for the top matching action if the LLM is not available. Before any action runs, the system checks its risk classification (read-only, mutating, or destructive) against the role's risk ceiling, and rejects anything above that threshold without even sending it to the executor—this is the first line of defense, with the global gate providing a second check underneath. The runner takes an agent ID, a goal statement, the full registry of available actions, an execution context dictionary, and optionally a list of forced steps for testing. It returns a detailed report including which steps were attempted, whether each succeeded, which ones were rejected by the risk ceiling, and an overall status. The code reads from control_plane.skills for the executor and gate logic, and calls control_plane.skills.registry for the lexical search fallback. Someone building permission systems around AI agents, implementing role-based access control, or investigating why certain actions were blocked by risk checks would look at this file.
control_plane/llm/server_client.py: This file acts as a thin HTTP client that talks to a long-running language model server over the network instead of starting a new model process each time a query arrives. The server runs separately (started by runtime/llama_server_run.cmd and kept alive in Windows Task Scheduler), holds the model in RAM permanently, and listens on port 8877 with a standard OpenAI-compatible API endpoint. The client is model-agnostic now: instead of manually building prompts in a specific format (ChatML), it sends standard messages to /v1/chat/completions, and the server itself applies whatever chat template is stored inside the model file (using the --jinja flag), so switching models requires no code changes. The generate_http function takes a system prompt string and user message string, plus optional parameters for maximum tokens and timeout duration, and returns a dictionary indicating success or failure: on success it contains the generated text, wall-clock time in seconds, and the mode; on any failure (network down, timeout, bad JSON, empty response) it returns an error dictionary and never raises an exception. The code also provides a quick health-check function that verifies the server is responding. Someone trying to speed up repeated queries to a language model, integrating a locally-hosted LLM into a larger system, or replacing one language model backend with another would use this file.
control_plane/operator/mouth.py: This file adds human-readable commentary to system incidents after the operator has already decided what to do, using a language model to briefly explain what probably happened and suggest a next step. The operator loop makes all decisions deterministically (about whether to restart services, scale up resources, or escalate to a human), and this module's only job is to attach a short, 1-2 sentence explanation that helps a human operator understand the context. The code is designed to never raise exceptions—any failure (missing model, LLM timeout, subprocess error, bad response) simply returns None, and the operator loop continues unchanged whether the commentary is present or not. It first tries to use a always-running Phi-4-mini server on port 8877 (via server_client.py) to avoid the overhead of loading the model fresh for each incident, and if that server is down or too slow, it falls back to running the model via subprocess (llama-cli.exe). The comment_incident function takes a dictionary containing issues and actions already decided by the deterministic operator, extracts the most important parts into a brief description (up to 5 issues and 5 actions), and sends that to the LLM with a system prompt requesting a concise comment in the language of the incident report if possible, otherwise in English. It returns the comment string or None if anything failed. Someone implementing human-friendly incident reporting, adding LLM commentary to automated system operations, or coordinating between deterministic rules and optional AI explanations would find this file useful.
control_plane/policy.py: This file defines which tools an operator is permitted to call and which commands are forbidden, acting as a simple allow-list and block-list system. The allowed_tools frozen set lists exactly seven tools that may be called: system_health, cbms_search, memory_recall, fast_search, aions_plan, aions_execute_step, and aions_execution_status; any other tool name is automatically blocked. The check_intent function screens user statements for dangerous patterns like 'rm -rf /', 'format c:', or 'delete all' and rejects any intent containing those substrings. Both functions return a tuple of (boolean, string) indicating whether the action is allowed and a reason message. There is no persistent state, network calls, or file I/O—this is purely an in-memory gate that can be checked before any action executes. Someone implementing a permission system for constrained execution, building policy controls for autonomous operations, or maintaining a list of blocked operations would consult this file.
control_plane/skills/semantic_search.py: This file enables finding the right action or skill by meaning, not just by matching words, by blending semantic similarity from vector embeddings with traditional keyword matching in a calibrated way. The module went through four iterations (v2 through v4) tuning weights and selecting embedders using a test set of 131 queries (48 original, plus 92 expanded with multilingual Polish cases, plus 39 new English cases), split once-and-frozen into tune and held-out evaluation halves. Each version improved on specific weaknesses: v2 fixed false positives by rejecting semantic-only candidates below a higher threshold; v3 tested a multilingual embedder but failed its accuracy gate (61.5% top-1 vs 64% bar); v4 achieved 87.5% on the held-out set by adding English descriptions and utterances to the indexed content while keeping the default embedder. The public semantic_skill_search function takes a query string and returns a list matching SkillRegistry.search's format, blending lexical token overlap (scored by term count, normalized to a saturation point) with semantic cosine similarity (0 to 1) using tuned weights, with separate acceptance thresholds for candidates found by both methods versus semantic-only candidates. Input data comes from the SkillRegistry (list of available skills with tags and descriptions) and the Chroma vector database (indexed documents with embeddings). Every Chroma call is wrapped in try/except, so if the database is down, the function silently degrades to pure keyword search. Someone building a skill finder that understands natural language paraphrases, tuning retrieval for multilingual queries, or investigating why a specific query matched or missed an expected skill would look at this file.
mcpServers/VS_CODE_MCP_CODEX/src/test_se: This file is the simplest possible test version of an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server, used to verify that the protocol works at all and the basic infrastructure is in place. It creates a FastMCP server instance, registers three trivial tools (ping returns pong, echo bounces back the message, and health returns server status), and runs via standard input/output transport. The main purpose is smoke-testing: confirming that the FastMCP library imported correctly, that tool registration works, and that the server can start and process basic requests. It prints debug messages to standard error at each step to help diagnose where something fails if it doesn't work. There is no persistent state, no database calls, and no external dependencies beyond the MCP server library. Someone new to the MCP server system, debugging why the integration isn't working, or setting up a minimal example to build from would start with this test server.
scripts/aions_tray.py: This file creates a small icon in the Windows system tray (the notification area in the bottom-right corner) that shows whether Claude Desktop is running and offers quick-access menu options to restart it, kill it, start it, open log files, or open the configuration file. The tray icon is green if Claude is running and red if it is not, with an 'A' for AIONS displayed inside. A background thread refreshes the icon status every 5 seconds so it always stays current. The right-click context menu provides six actions: Restart Claude Desktop, Stop Claude Desktop, Start Claude Desktop, Open Logs, Open Config, and Exit Tray Manager. The code finds Claude.exe in the standard Windows location (LocalAppData\Programs\Claude), checks running processes using psutil to detect whether Claude is already running or not, and launches or kills it using subprocess calls. The log file path is read from environment variables (Claude's logs folder), and the configuration file is looked for in the AppData\Claude directory. Someone needing quick controls to restart Claude without using the command line, monitoring whether Claude is still running, or accessing Claude's logs and configuration without hunting for folders would use this script.
scripts/demo_secretary.py: This script shows the skill engine in action by running a practical workflow: a morning status briefing, a system notification popup, learning a new multi-step recipe by example, opening Gmail in the browser, testing skill retrieval on real queries, and showing a summary of performance. The workflow demonstrates building a context object (workspace for state), discovering available skills from the library, executing individual skills in sequence (get current time, system info, open windows, recent files, RAM usage, send notification), running a multi-step chain to create a note with the current timestamp and count its words, saving that chain as a reusable recipe if it succeeded, and searching for skills by intent (e.g., 'co mam otwarte' for 'what do I have open'). It reads from a skills library, builds an execution context, runs skills through an executor with verification steps, stores successful sequences as recipes, and prints statistics about how many skills succeeded and how many recipes are available. Someone learning how to use the skills engine, testing whether skills work end-to-end, or understanding what multi-step workflows look like would read this script.
scripts/proof_provenance.py: This script acts as a smoke test to verify that every piece of information stored in memory carries audit metadata (where it came from, who stored it, which machine, which session, when). It connects to the MCP server via HTTP, calls the memory_store tool with a test message, then queries the ChromaDB database directly to retrieve the metadata for that stored record and checks that all six required fields are present: agent (which system wrote it), host (which computer), surface (which interface), run_id (which execution), os (operating system), and era (timestamp). It exits with code 0 only if all required fields are found, making it suitable for use in automated deployment pipelines. The test writes through the live HTTP endpoint but reads directly from ChromaDB by importing the chromadb library, so it verifies the full path from API to storage layer. Someone implementing a compliance or audit system, verifying that metadata capture is working, or testing memory storage before deployment would run this script.
server/store_api.py: This file provides a thin wrapper around a remote vector database API, presenting an HTTP interface to a FastAPI server on localhost:8765 as if it were a local vector database object. It mirrors the embedded vector database interface so callers can use the same method names (add_items, search, session_stats, prune_expired, etc.) without knowing whether the data is being stored locally or on a remote server. The VectorStore class takes an optional API base URL (defaulting to http://127.0.0.1:8765 from environment variable AIONS_API_BASE_URL) and makes HTTP POST or GET requests for every operation: adding items to a session, searching a session with a query and optional metadata filters, listing sessions, checking health, pruning expired records, getting a dashboard summary, and retrieving status. All network requests wrap errors into RuntimeError exceptions so callers know if something went wrong without needing to handle HTTP-specific exceptions. Someone integrating a vector database server into a system that needs to run in multiple places, separating the database layer from application code, or wanting to query AIONS data from outside processes would use this API client.
